# Task 49: continuous scroll reader (no Begin gate, no wheel page turns)

Repo martinmw13/LectorIA-meta, worktree /workspace/wt-49, branch `continuous-scroll` (from latest main). Read AGENTS.md first and follow every repo rule (co-author trailer via the hook, file-size hook, check:secrets, isolation). No paid API calls, do not touch data/. Keep the diff focused on the reader: other agents own app/skin.ts, app/use-skin.ts, app/rain-button.tsx, app/icons*.tsx, app/tokens.css, app/styles/ambience.css (rain v2 / skin seam, PR #48) and the Picture this drawing animations (app/folio/image-pane.tsx visuals). Do not edit those files beyond a one-line prop/call change if strictly required.

## Owner feedback (Martin, verbatim, Spanish)
"el scroll no anda fluido. Por otro lado, no me gusta que cada capítulo tenga el botón de Begin the Chapter. Quiero que ya aparezca el texto. Está bien que esté ahí esa tira que diga Chapter in Panels, pero quiero que ya empiece el texto y yo simplemente le scrollear si quiero ignorar el Chapter in Panels."

## Today
app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx renders one scene per route; app/leer/scene-page.tsx paginates the scene into sub-pages (chapter cover with "Begin the chapter →" + "or just scroll", text pages, end page with "Relive this chapter in panels" / "On to Chapter N →"), hijacks wheel/trackpad to turn pages (app/folio/scroll-turn.ts, PR #37), and keys turn pages. Cues "Turn the page ↓", "Next scene ↓", "Finish Chapter N ↓" (readOnLabel). app/reader.tsx (layout) drives the music session from the route scene id (useParams), and shows chapter/scene progress. The .read-col is the scrolling element.

## Goal
Native, smooth, momentum CONTINUOUS SCROLL through the whole book, organised by scene:
1. The reading column renders the whole book (all chapters, all scenes, all paragraphs) as one long scroll. Each chapter starts with its kicker/number + chapter title + the existing Chapter in panels strip (PanelsOfferCard / PanelsQuietLink, spoiler gate kept) inline, immediately followed by the chapter text. No Begin button, no "or just scroll" hint. Scene boundaries are natural breaks (a section per scene, e.g. `<section data-scene-id>` with a light divider/ornament between scenes; keep the "Scene k of n" line subtle or drop it if it adds noise). At a chapter's end keep a light "Relive this chapter in panels" entry inline (no full-screen end page) and the text simply continues into the next chapter. Book end shows "The end."
2. Delete the wheel hijacking (scene-page wheel listener, inNestedScroller, wheelState, app/folio/scroll-turn.ts and its test if nothing else uses it), the paged sub-page model in the reader UI (pagination, enterAtEnd, readOn cues, sub-page progress), and the keyboard page-turn handler. Space / PageDown / PageUp / arrows / Home / End work through NATIVE scrolling: make sure the scroll container is the thing that receives keys (either let the document/body scroll, or keep .read-col as scroller but focus it on load with tabIndex=-1 and no focus ring). Prefer whatever gives true native momentum on trackpads and the least code. Remove now-dead pure helpers in core/reader (paginateScene, subPageCount, navReducer, etc.) only if no other caller and tests remain, else leave them.
3. Current scene = the scene section most in view, tracked with ONE IntersectionObserver (no scroll listeners doing layout reads; if any scroll listener is unavoidable it must be passive and rAF-throttled). The current scene id drives: music sceneEntered transitions in app/reader.tsx (keep the existing session dwell/gate semantics), the Picture this scene card + selection popover anchored to the scene in view (never offered on a chapter heading/strip area), the vault, the BandPager/progress ("scene x of y"), and the URL: update it with `window.history.replaceState` to `/leer/<sceneId>` (Next 16 syncs native history with usePathname/useParams; verify Reader sees it — if not, share current scene via a tiny context/store instead). Do not router.push per scene (no remounts while scrolling).
4. Resume: loading /leer/<sceneId> scrolls instantly (no animation) to that scene's section; also remember the last scene in localStorage (key under the existing namespace style) and, when landing on /leer/c1s1 or /read/oz with nothing explicit... keep it simple: only the URL is required; localStorage resume is optional, skip if it complicates.
5. BandPager prev/next and chapter jumps: scroll to the target section (smooth unless prefers-reduced-motion, then instant). All programmatic smooth scrolling respects prefers-reduced-motion.
6. Perf: no layout thrash on scroll. Lazy images (`loading="lazy" decoding="async"` on inline figures / panel thumbs). Add `content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 1200px` (or similar) on scene sections so a full book stays smooth; check that IntersectionObserver and anchor scrolling still work with it (contain-intrinsic-size `auto` keeps remembered sizes). Remove any CSS scroll-snap / scroll-behavior that fights momentum.
7. Narration auto-follow (for the narration UI another agent is building on top of PR #46 word timings): export a small helper, e.g. `followIntoView(el, scroller)` in app/leer/ or app/folio/, that scrolls the spoken word into view only when it leaves a comfortable band, and pauses auto-follow for ~4 s after any user wheel/touch/key scroll (passive listeners). Unit test it. Do not build the narration UI.
8. Picture this: usePictures currently takes one sceneId. Make it work per scene in view (simplest: pass the current scene id; figures/popover attach to the text container of that scene; selections in another scene switch the current scene). Keep the PR #42 callback-ref behaviour. Picture this is never offered on chapter headings.
9. Server payload: app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx should build the whole-book view once (static params stay one route per scene so deep links and prerendering work); remove the per-route `key={sceneId}` remount. Keep the existing rule that the client gets only text it renders. If the shared page HTML is large that is acceptable (one book).

## Tests and e2e
- Update/replace unit tests that covered paging/wheel turns; add tests for the current-scene picking logic (pure function: given intersection ratios/positions -> scene id) and followIntoView.
- Rewrite scripts/e2e-scroll.py (opt-in, Python Playwright; keep the skip-if-missing behaviour and CLI). At 1440x900 and 1280x800 it must assert: (a) on /leer/c1s1 there is NO "Begin the chapter" button and chapter-1 paragraph text is visible in the viewport right away (the panels strip may be above it); (b) trackpad-like wheel input alone (no clicks) scrolls continuously and reaches chapter 2+ (URL becomes /leer/c2s… and a c2 paragraph is in view) and keeps going to chapter 3, with the URL scene id changing monotonically; (c) frame timing is smooth while wheel-scrolling: measure requestAnimationFrame deltas in-page during the scroll and assert p95 frame delta <= 34 ms and no frame > 100 ms in headless Chromium (print the stats); (d) Space and PageDown scroll down (scrollTop increases), PageUp scrolls back; (e) no page errors; (f) #scene-heading/headings show no focus ring. Save screenshots to a directory given by $SHOTS_DIR when set.
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run check:secrets`, `npm run check:size`, `npm run check:isolation`, `npm run test:hooks`, `npm run build` must pass. Then run `npx next start -p 3049` in the background, run `python3 scripts/e2e-scroll.py http://localhost:3049` (CHROME_PATH may be set), fix failures, and stop the server.

## Docs
Write docs/tasks/49-continuous-scroll.md (short design), docs/reviews/49.md (what changed, decisions, verification results incl. frame stats), one line in BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md. Update any docs/contracts note that describes the paged reader. Commit in small logical commits with clear messages (hook adds the trailer). Do not push.

Use the `ponytail-review` skill on your own diff before finishing. End with: what you skipped and any risk.

Read text file `AGENTS.md`.
1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.
2|
3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary. Scenes split at strong sequential emotion shifts; blends stay in the vector.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary. Scenes split at strong sequential emotion shifts; blends stay in the vector.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

# Durable Test Collateral

Verification is part of the delivered project when it can prevent the same
behavior from breaking again. Use the project's existing framework and
conventions.

Loading this skill does not mean the current turn asked for the change. While you
are still investigating — explaining existing behavior, or answering a design
question the user raised — use commands that only read and leave the repository
unmodified, tests included.

## Scale to the task

Skip the failing-test-first workflow below when the change is tiny and leaves
program logic alone (a typo, a text or style tweak, a config value, or a version
pin), when the work is a throwaway prototype or a standalone one-file script or
page, when the request adds features to a project you created earlier in this
session, or when the user asks for speed or a quick result. A quick direct check
of the changed behavior is enough there; if you add no maintained test, say so in
the report. A user request for tests anywhere in the session, or a
specification that makes tests a deliverable, still applies.

Any other bug fix or behavior change keeps the workflow at its smallest: one
focused failing test, the fix, that test passing, and, when a broad run is
required, one broad run after the final edit. A report that something already
built behaves wrongly is a bug fix, even when it comes with feature requests.

Before a test run that may take more than a minute or two, tell the user in one
line what runs and why. If you poll it, post a short status line between polls;
never poll a long run silently.

## Keep the check with the project

For a bug fix or behavior change, add or update the smallest maintained test in
the repository's normal test layout that exercises the changed behavior. If a
specification makes a reusable suite or test category a deliverable, implement
that suite instead of treating it as private verification.

An inline interpreter command, heredoc, scratch script, temporary-directory
test, demo, or manual probe may help diagnose the problem, but it does not
replace the maintained test. Keep a useful self-authored test unless the user
explicitly asks for a disposable probe.

Do not add a new test framework solely to satisfy this skill. If the repository
has no maintained harness and the request does not require one, disclose when
durable coverage would be disproportionate or infeasible and use the narrowest
honest verification instead.

On a later turn, update the maintained test even when the old suite remains
green and the user does not repeat the test request. Cover the new behavior,
not merely an unrelated cleanup in the test file.

## Prove the maintained check

Observe the authentic failure before the implementation change when it is safe
and runnable. Then make the smallest implementation change and run the focused

"""Opt-in end-to-end check for wheel/trackpad/keyboard page turns (not run in CI).

Usage: python3 scripts/e2e-scroll.py [base_url]  (default http://localhost:3000)
Browser: $CHROME_PATH when set, else Playwright's bundled Chromium.
Needs Python Playwright; when it is not importable this prints a skip and exits 0.
Exits 1 with a clear message on the first failed assertion.

At 1440x900 and 1280x800 it asserts:
(a) trackpad-style swipes from /leer/c1s1 advance exactly one page each
    (every swipe yields a new, never-repeated label) and reach c2s1
    within 20 swipes;
(b) Space, PageDown and ArrowDown each advance a page and PageUp goes back;
(c) no page errors;
(d) after arriving at c2s1 by wheel, #scene-heading has computed
    outline-style "none" (or outline-width 0px).
"""

import os
import sys

try:
    from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
except ImportError:
    print("skip: python playwright is not installed (pip install playwright)")
    sys.exit(0)

VIEWPORTS = [(1440, 900), (1280, 800)]
MAX_SWIPES = 20


def fail(msg):
    print(f"FAIL: {msg}", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)


def scene_of(page):
    return page.url.rstrip("/").split("/")[-1].split("?")[0].split("#")[0]


def label(page):
    if page.locator(".scene-line").count():
        text = page.locator(".scene-line").first.inner_text()
    elif page.locator(".kicker").count():
        text = page.locator(".kicker").first.inner_text()
    else:
        text = ""
    return (scene_of(page), " ".join(text.split()))


def swipe(page):
    # Trackpad-like swipe: 40 decaying wheel events, 16ms apart (inertia).
    for i in range(40):
        page.mouse.wheel(0, max(2, int(60 * (0.92**i))))
        page.wait_for_timeout(16)
    page.wait_for_timeout(500)


def press_advance(page, key, prev, tag):
    # Space/Page/arrow keys scroll tall columns before turning, so allow
    # a few presses; the key must still move to a new page.
    for _ in range(3):
        page.keyboard.press(key)
        page.wait_for_timeout(700)
        now = label(page)
        if now != prev:
            return now
    fail(f"[{tag}] {key} did not advance after 3 presses (stuck at {prev})")


def check_viewport(browser, base, w, h):
    tag = f"{w}x{h}"
    page = browser.new_page(viewport={"width": w, "height": h})
    errors = []
    page.on("pageerror", lambda e: errors.append(str(e)))
    try:
        # (a) wheel sweep from the chapter-1 cover to chapter 2.
        page.goto(f"{base}/leer/c1s1", wait_until="networkidle")
        page.wait_for_timeout(1000)
        if scene_of(page) != "c1s1":
            fail(f"[{tag}] expected to start at /leer/c1s1, got {page.url}")

# Task 49: continuous scroll reader (no Begin gate, no wheel page turns)

Repo martinmw13/LectorIA-meta, worktree /workspace/wt-49, branch `continuous-scroll` (from latest main). Read AGENTS.md first and follow every repo rule (co-author trailer via the hook, file-size hook, check:secrets, isolation). No paid API calls, do not touch data/. Keep the diff focused on the reader: other agents own app/skin.ts, app/use-skin.ts, app/rain-button.tsx, app/icons*.tsx, app/tokens.css, app/styles/ambience.css (rain v2 / skin seam, PR #48) and the Picture this drawing animations (app/folio/image-pane.tsx visuals). Do not edit those files beyond a one-line prop/call change if strictly required.

## Owner feedback (Martin, verbatim, Spanish)
"el scroll no anda fluido. Por otro lado, no me gusta que cada capítulo tenga el botón de Begin the Chapter. Quiero que ya aparezca el texto. Está bien que esté ahí esa tira que diga Chapter in Panels, pero quiero que ya empiece el texto y yo simplemente le scrollear si quiero ignorar el Chapter in Panels."

## Today
app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx renders one scene per route; app/leer/scene-page.tsx paginates the scene into sub-pages (chapter cover with "Begin the chapter →" + "or just scroll", text pages, end page with "Relive this chapter in panels" / "On to Chapter N →"), hijacks wheel/trackpad to turn pages (app/folio/scroll-turn.ts, PR #37), and keys turn pages. Cues "Turn the page ↓", "Next scene ↓", "Finish Chapter N ↓" (readOnLabel). app/reader.tsx (layout) drives the music session from the route scene id (useParams), and shows chapter/scene progress. The .read-col is the scrolling element.

## Goal
Native, smooth, momentum CONTINUOUS SCROLL through the whole book, organised by scene:
1. The reading column renders the whole book (all chapters, all scenes, all paragraphs) as one long scroll. Each chapter starts with its kicker/number + chapter title + the existing Chapter in panels strip (PanelsOfferCard / PanelsQuietLink, spoiler gate kept) inline, immediately followed by the chapter text. No Begin button, no "or just scroll" hint. Scene boundaries are natural breaks (a section per scene, e.g. `<section data-scene-id>` with a light divider/ornament between scenes; keep the "Scene k of n" line subtle or drop it if it adds noise). At a chapter's end keep a light "Relive this chapter in panels" entry inline (no full-screen end page) and the text simply continues into the next chapter. Book end shows "The end."
2. Delete the wheel hijacking (scene-page wheel listener, inNestedScroller, wheelState, app/folio/scroll-turn.ts and its test if nothing else uses it), the paged sub-page model in the reader UI (pagination, enterAtEnd, readOn cues, sub-page progress), and the keyboard page-turn handler. Space / PageDown / PageUp / arrows / Home / End work through NATIVE scrolling: make sure the scroll container is the thing that receives keys (either let the document/body scroll, or keep .read-col as scroller but focus it on load with tabIndex=-1 and no focus ring). Prefer whatever gives true native momentum on trackpads and the least code. Remove now-dead pure helpers in core/reader (paginateScene, subPageCount, navReducer, etc.) only if no other caller and tests remain, else leave them.
3. Current scene = the scene section most in view, tracked with ONE IntersectionObserver (no scroll listeners doing layout reads; if any scroll listener is unavoidable it must be passive and rAF-throttled). The current scene id drives: music sceneEntered transitions in app/reader.tsx (keep the existing session dwell/gate semantics), the Picture this scene card + selection popover anchored to the scene in view (never offered on a chapter heading/strip area), the vault, the BandPager/progress ("scene x of y"), and the URL: update it with `window.history.replaceState` to `/leer/<sceneId>` (Next 16 syncs native history with usePathname/useParams; verify Reader sees it — if not, share current scene via a tiny context/store instead). Do not router.push per scene (no remounts while scrolling).
4. Resume: loading /leer/<sceneId> scrolls instantly (no animation) to that scene's section; also remember the last scene in localStorage (key under the existing namespace style) and, when landing on /leer/c1s1 or /read/oz with nothing explicit... keep it simple: only the URL is required; localStorage resume is optional, skip if it complicates.
5. BandPager prev/next and chapter jumps: scroll to the target section (smooth unless prefers-reduced-motion, then instant). All programmatic smooth scrolling respects prefers-reduced-motion.
6. Perf: no layout thrash on scroll. Lazy images (`loading="lazy" decoding="async"` on inline figures / panel thumbs). Add `content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 1200px` (or similar) on scene sections so a full book stays smooth; check that IntersectionObserver and anchor scrolling still work with it (contain-intrinsic-size `auto` keeps remembered sizes). Remove any CSS scroll-snap / scroll-behavior that fights momentum.
7. Narration auto-follow (for the narration UI another agent is building on top of PR #46 word timings): export a small helper, e.g. `followIntoView(el, scroller)` in app/leer/ or app/folio/, that scrolls the spoken word into view only when it leaves a comfortable band, and pauses auto-follow for ~4 s after any user wheel/touch/key scroll (passive listeners). Unit test it. Do not build the narration UI.
8. Picture this: usePictures currently takes one sceneId. Make it work per scene in view (simplest: pass the current scene id; figures/popover attach to the text container of that scene; selections in another scene switch the current scene). Keep the PR #42 callback-ref behaviour. Picture this is never offered on chapter headings.
9. Server payload: app/leer/[sceneId]/page.tsx should build the whole-book view once (static params stay one route per scene so deep links and prerendering work); remove the per-route `key={sceneId}` remount. Keep the existing rule that the client gets only text it renders. If the shared page HTML is large that is acceptable (one book).

## Tests and e2e
- Update/replace unit tests that covered paging/wheel turns; add tests for the current-scene picking logic (pure function: given intersection ratios/positions -> scene id) and followIntoView.
- Rewrite scripts/e2e-scroll.py (opt-in, Python Playwright; keep the skip-if-missing behaviour and CLI). At 1440x900 and 1280x800 it must assert: (a) on /leer/c1s1 there is NO "Begin the chapter" button and chapter-1 paragraph text is visible in the viewport right away (the panels strip may be above it); (b) trackpad-like wheel input alone (no clicks) scrolls continuously and reaches chapter 2+ (URL becomes /leer/c2s… and a c2 paragraph is in view) and keeps going to chapter 3, with the URL scene id changing monotonically; (c) frame timing is smooth while wheel-scrolling: measure requestAnimationFrame deltas in-page during the scroll and assert p95 frame delta <= 34 ms and no frame > 100 ms in headless Chromium (print the stats); (d) Space and PageDown scroll down (scrollTop increases), PageUp scrolls back; (e) no page errors; (f) #scene-heading/headings show no focus ring. Save screenshots to a directory given by $SHOTS_DIR when set.
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run check:secrets`, `npm run check:size`, `npm run check:isolation`, `npm run test:hooks`, `npm run build` must pass. Then run `npx next start -p 3049` in the background, run `python3 scripts/e2e-scroll.py http://localhost:3049` (CHROME_PATH may be set), fix failures, and stop the server.

## Docs
Write docs/tasks/49-continuous-scroll.md (short design), docs/reviews/49.md (what changed, decisions, verification results incl. frame stats), one line in BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md. Update any docs/contracts note that describes the paged reader. Commit in small logical commits with clear messages (hook adds the trailer). Do not push.

---
name: ponytail-review
description: >
  Quality review of a change: is the logic right, is it safe, does it hold
  under real load, is risky code tested, is it fast enough, and is every line
  needed. Reads the connected code, not only the diff. Each finding is
  explained in plain English. Use for "review this", "code review", "review
  the last commit", "review my PR", "is this over-engineered", /ponytail-review.
---

Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.

## 1. Understand first

- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
  if there are none.
- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
  that, and say which load you assumed.

## 2. Look for

1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
   caller while the shared function stays broken.
2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
   wrong order, no transaction).
3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
   test, not coverage.
5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)
   - stdlib / native: the standard library or platform already does it; a
     new dependency for a few lines
   - yagni: abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets
   - merge: near-copies that must change together
   - split: one function doing several unrelated jobs, so it is hard to read
     or test. Split by job, never by line count, and never into helpers that
     exist only to make a function shorter.

## 3. Check before you report

- Every finding needs a concrete case: "this input or situation leads to this
  wrong result". No case, no finding.
- Re-read the lines and confirm: the caller exists, the value can really be
  empty, the code really is unused.
- A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a
  decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it.
- Propose the smallest fix that works. Prefer fixes that delete code. Never
  add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
- No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.

## 4. Output

Very simple English: short sentences, everyday words. Explain a technical
term the first time you use it. The reader may never have seen this code.

Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences.

Then the findings in three groups, skip empty groups:
- **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load.
- **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a
  function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist.
- **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.

Number findings across all groups, so the user can say "fix 2 and 5".
Every finding has all four parts, each one or two short sentences:

2. **Orders land on the wrong day** (`billing/close_day.py:L40-52`)
   - **What this is:** At midnight this job closes the day and bills all orders of that day.
   - **Problem:** It takes "today" from the server clock, which runs in UTC. An order placed
     at 00:30 in Berlin is billed on the day before.
   - **Fix:** Compute the day once in the shop's time zone:
     `datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")).date()`. One line, nothing else changes.
   - **If we skip it:** Late orders show the wrong date, and accounting fixes them by hand.

End with:
- `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`
- `Lean: -<N> lines possible.` when lean findings exist.
- `Not checked:` one line, if something mattered and you could not check it.

Nothing found: `What this change does:`, then `Looks good. Ship.` and one line
on what you checked.

Lists findings, changes no code.

</skill-body>

# Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

Restore first saves the current workspace, leaves HEAD, branch, and the real
index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

## Always fine

Read-only inspection such as `status`, `log`, `show`, `diff`, `blame`,
`branch -v`, `show-ref`, `rev-parse`, `for-each-ref`, and `merge-base` is fine.
Staging named files to inspect `diff --cached`, and a temporary stash around a
tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.
- Do not create or edit `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` to hide the user's
  files, and do not stash the user's files (including `stash push -u`) to make
  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and
  similar phrasing do not authorize committing, pushing, ignoring, excluding,
  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.

</read-skill-result>

Done. The reader is one native continuous scroll now, committed in 6 small commits on `continuous-scroll`, not pushed.

What this change does: every `/leer/<sceneId>` route ships the whole book as a single column (chapter header + panels strip inline, then text, one `section[data-scene-id]` per scene). The scene most in view — one IntersectionObserver, max-ratio picking — drives pictures, vault, pager, music, and the URL via `replaceState`. No Begin gate, no sub-pages, no wheel/key hijacking.

**Must fix:** none found. Leftover scan for `Begin the chapter`, `scroll-turn`, `navReducer`, `subPage`, `ScenePage`, `cover-begin`, `read-on` is clean.

**Should fix:** none open. Two lean merges applied during review (`gotoScene` shared by pager and chapter-jump events; pager handlers simplified).

1. **Cross-scene figure race** ([app/folio/use-pictures.ts](/workspace/wt-49/app/folio/use-pictures.ts)): a passage request started in scene A that resolves after scrolling to B appends to B's live list but stays invisible (ordinal mismatch) until A is revisited, when the cache resync restores it. Self-heals, 3-second window, rare.
